## Support Vector Machine

Support Vector Regression (SVR) provides the second demand-prediction approach.
It predicts trip count for Community Areas [@chicagoCommunityAreas], Census
Tracts [@chicagoCensusTracts] and H3 hexagons [@uberH3] at one-, four- and
twenty-four-hour resolutions. The models use the previously described
temporal, weather [@iowaMesonetASOS], holiday and point-of-interest features. To
provide one spatial representation across all three unit types, unit centroids
are converted from longitude and latitude to spherical coordinates. The final scikit-learn pipeline [@sklearn_api; @pedregosa2011scikit] scales inputs and the target,
compares linear SVR with kernel approximations and uses successive-halving model
selection. Kernel approximation, caching and restricted search spaces make the
large data sets computationally tractable. GPU training with cuML
[@rapids_cuml; @raschka2020machine] was also evaluated, but project runs on larger samples produced
unstable results. The pipeline and this implementation-specific observation are
documented in the Appendix.

### Results

![Test-metric comparison of SVR and the three baseline models.](./report_assets/figures/main/svm_baseline_comparison.png){#fig-svm-baseline-comparison width=80%}

Across configurations, SVR generally outperforms the zero and global-median
baselines but remains behind the spatial-time-weekday mean
(@fig-svm-baseline-comparison). The H3 resolution 7 four-hour model performs best
relative to this strongest baseline, although the difference is small. The high
share of zero-demand observations is a central limitation: aggregate errors can
be dominated by easy zero cases, while sparse non-zero cases make model
selection and fitting less stable.

![SVR metrics across spatial and temporal configurations.](./report_assets/figures/main/svm_heatmap.png){#fig-svm-resolution-heatmap width=80%}

The hexagonal representations provide the strongest overall results
(@fig-svm-resolution-heatmap). H3 resolution 8 has lower absolute errors, whereas
the coarser H3 resolution 7 performs better on $R^2$. Census Tracts have the
weakest $R^2$, while Community Areas have the highest MAE and RMSE. Shorter time
intervals generally perform better; the Community Area model is particularly
weak at the twenty-four-hour resolution.

### SVC

An exploratory Support Vector Classification (SVC) model maps demand to five
data-informed but fixed classes: zero, low, medium, high and very high. Training
uses class balancing to prevent zero demand from dominating. Performance was not
strong enough to justify further development, and any operational application
would require retuning the class boundaries; the exploratory result is shown in
@fig-svc-classification-results in the Appendix.

### Further Improvement

Future work should first remove spatial units outside the operational area and
evaluate the remaining zero-demand structure explicitly. Suitable alternatives
include a two-stage classifier-regressor such as `ZeroInflatedRegressor`
[@vincent_d_warmerdam_2026_21210295] or a count model such as
`ZeroInflatedPoisson` [@josef_perktold_2024_10984387]. Model families should be
screened on representative samples before full fitting so that computationally
infeasible candidates are rejected early. Given the observed convergence,
runtime and predictive performance, SVMs are not recommended as the primary
model family for this demand data.

## NN compared to SVM

We compare both models on the same TEST observations. The NN performs better on most error metrics and has higher precision. The SVM achieves higher recall across all configurations. It detects more demand intervals, but it also produces more false demand signals. The NN is more conservative, although the SVM performs better on several metrics for H3 resolution 7 at 24 hours. The number of metric wins is reported in @tbl-final-nn-svm-metric-wins.
The demand bucket comparison provides a more detailed view. For Census Tracts at 1 hour, the SVM has slightly lower MAE for intervals with 1 or 2 to 3 trips. The NN performs better from 4 trips onwards. Its advantage grows at high demand. These results are shown in @fig-final-census-tract-1h-demand-bucket-mae. The complete comparison across datasets is presented in @fig-final-nn-svm-pipeline-comparison.
Both models usually improve on the always zero prediction. This is a weak benchmark because it does not support useful fleet operations. The stronger spatial × time × weekday baseline is only outperformed by the NN for Census Tracts at 1 hour. With the current data and features, the additional complexity of both model pipelines creates little operational value.

```{python}
#| label: fig-final-mae-skill-trivial-baselines
#| fig-cap: "Test MAE skill scores of NN and SVM models against both baselines."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-align: center

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

comparison_metrics_path = Path(
    "results/appendix/svm_nn_model_metrics.parquet"
)
if not comparison_metrics_path.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Missing NN-SVM comparison metrics: {comparison_metrics_path}. "
        "Run the NN-SVM comparison notebook before rendering the report."
    )

skill_metrics = pd.read_parquet(
    comparison_metrics_path,
    columns=[
        "dataset",
        "model",
        "mae_skill_vs_zero",
        "mae_skill_vs_spatial_time_weekday_mean",
    ],
)
dataset_order = [
    "census_tracts_1h",
    "census_tracts_4h",
    "census_tracts_24h",
    "community_areas_1h",
    "community_areas_4h",
    "community_areas_24h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_1h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_4h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_24h",
]
dataset_labels = {
    "census_tracts_1h": "Census tracts · 1H",
    "census_tracts_4h": "Census tracts · 4H",
    "census_tracts_24h": "Census tracts · 24H",
    "community_areas_1h": "Community areas · 1H",
    "community_areas_4h": "Community areas · 4H",
    "community_areas_24h": "Community areas · 24H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_1h": "H3 resolution 7 · 1H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_4h": "H3 resolution 7 · 4H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_24h": "H3 resolution 7 · 24H",
}
expected_pairs = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [dataset_order, ["NN", "SVM"]],
    names=["dataset", "model"],
)
actual_pairs = pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(
    skill_metrics[["dataset", "model"]]
)
if (
    len(expected_pairs.difference(actual_pairs))
    or skill_metrics.duplicated(["dataset", "model"]).any()
):
    raise ValueError(
        "Expected exactly one NN and one SVM row for every dataset."
    )

plot_specs = [
    (
        "mae_skill_vs_zero",
        "MAE skill vs. zero-demand baseline",
    ),
    (
        "mae_skill_vs_spatial_time_weekday_mean",
        "MAE skill vs. spatial × time × weekday baseline",
    ),
]
model_colors = {
    "NN": "#1f77b4",
    "SVM": "#ff7f0e",
}
dataset_positions = np.arange(len(dataset_order))
bar_width = 0.38

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    2,
    1,
    figsize=(13.5, 9.5),
    sharex=True,
    constrained_layout=True,
)
for axis, (metric, title) in zip(axes, plot_specs):
    for offset, model in (
        (-bar_width / 2, "NN"),
        (bar_width / 2, "SVM"),
    ):
        values = (
            skill_metrics.loc[
                lambda frame: frame["model"].eq(model),
                ["dataset", metric],
            ]
            .set_index("dataset")
            .reindex(dataset_order)[metric]
            .to_numpy()
        )
        axis.bar(
            dataset_positions + offset,
            values,
            bar_width,
            label=model,
            color=model_colors[model],
        )

    axis.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
    axis.set_title(title, loc="left")
    axis.set_ylabel("MAE skill score")
    axis.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1.0))
    axis.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
    axis.legend(frameon=False, ncols=2)

axes[-1].set_xticks(dataset_positions)
axes[-1].set_xticklabels(
    [dataset_labels[dataset] for dataset in dataset_order],
    rotation=35,
    ha="right",
)
figure.suptitle(
    "MAE skill scores by model and dataset",
    fontsize=15,
)
plt.show()
```

For the pilot, we therefore recommend the spatial × time × weekday baseline. It is simple, transparent and inexpensive to maintain. The current NN and SVM pipelines should not be used as the only basis for fleet dispatch. This result does not show that NNs are generally better than SVMs. It only applies to the pipelines and data evaluated in this report. A follow up project with additional information and a model designed for different demand levels may provide more value.
